summary:
EmberTrace is a web application that turns more than 43 million NASA FIRMS fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for Southeast Asia, from 2003 to today. MODIS holds over 20 years of fire history but is nearing the end of its life, while VIIRS is sharper but only starts in 2012, and the two sensors count fire differently. 

EmberTrace harmonizes them: it counts fire as cell-days on a shared 0.05° grid and converts MODIS to VIIRS-equivalent terms with a factor fitted per area and month. On years the calibration never saw, the result matches VIIRS with r = 0.997 and a bias of −4.6%. 

Users draw any area on the map and see which months burn, which years were worst, how this month compares with the same days in past years, what kind of land is burning, and an experimental three-month outlook, all downloadable as CSV. This matters because emergency managers need a fast, trustworthy answer to “is this fire season unusual here?”.
details:
EmberTrace is a web application that turns more than 43 million NASA FIRMS active-fire detections into one consistent record of burning activity for Southeast Asia, from 2003 to today. It combines the long MODIS history (Terra and Aqua, Collection 6.1) with the sharper VIIRS record (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, 375 m). Fire is counted as cell-days on a 0.05° grid, so differences in pixel size between the two sensors stop mattering. For 2013–2017, when both sensors flew, we measured how many VIIRS cell-days each MODIS cell-day represents, separately for each area and month, using Empirical Bayes shrinkage so areas with few fires borrow strength from the region. MODIS years are then converted to VIIRS-equivalent terms, giving one continuous series. Users draw any area up to 500,000 km², or pick a preset such as Central Kalimantan, and see a burning calendar of every month since 2003. They can also compare the current month with the same days in past years, see the share of fire in forest, farmland and other land using MODIS land cover (MCD12Q1), and view an experimental three-month fire outlook on a 15 km grid. Everything can be downloaded as CSV, Parquet or PNG.

Without harmonization, fire counts jump in 2012 simply because VIIRS started. With it, a jump means something really changed. On years the calibration never saw (2018–2021), the harmonized series matches VIIRS with a correlation of r = 0.997 and a bias of −4.6%. In back-tests over 2015–2025, the 10% of cells the outlook ranked highest held 62% of the following month’s fire. The tool already shows what it’s for: 2026 is Central Kalimantan’s biggest fire year since 2015, with 47,005 hotspots by 14 November, and the first half of November ran at about seven times the usual level, mostly in forest. The intended impact is to give emergency responders a fast answer to “is this month unusual here?”, scientists one record across two generations of satellites, and land managers a way to compare areas, periods and land types.

We built the project with Python, DuckDB and Apache Parquet for the data pipeline, a Flask API that answers each request on the server, and a React, TypeScript and Leaflet front end, with Chart.js for the charts. Heavy analysis runs on the server, so the browser receives small summaries instead of millions of points.

The project treats harmonization as the product, not a hidden preprocessing step. It rebuilds two satellites’ records into one, then asks new questions of the result: is this month unusual, which kind of land is burning, and where does fire usually come next? We considered both scientific honesty and usability. Pre-2012 values are labelled as estimates with their error range. The Methods tab shows the calibration and its test, and every calendar cell shows its number so color isn’t the only cue. The outlook is based on past fire patterns, not weather. Near-real-time data can include a few industrial heat sources. Degraded peat often maps as farmland rather than forest.
